t: Basarab I's victory over Charles I of Hungary at the Battle of Posada in 1330 consolidated Wallachia as an independent principality.
Wallachia accepted Ottoman suzerainty in 1417 and kept it until the mid-nineteenth century, yet preserved its own princes, boyars and Orthodox Church throughout.
Slavery of Roma, attested from 1385, was part of Wallachian society until the law of February 1856 freed all slaves as taxpayers.
dyk: The Transylvanian Saxons, angered when Vlad III strengthened Wallachia's borders and disrupted their trade routes, spread grotesque poems painting him as a drinker of blood; those tales inspired the main character of Bram Stoker's Dracula in 1897.
ev: Basarab I refuses tribute to Charles I of Hungary and decisively defeats his invasion at the Battle of Posada, consolidating the Wallachian state.
After Mehmed I takes Turnu Măgurele and Giurgiu, Mircea I accepts a peace treaty and Wallachia submits to Ottoman suzerainty for the first time.
Vlad III the Impaler is defeated by Mehmed the Conqueror after the Night Attack at Târgoviște and must accept an increased tribute.
Michael the Brave, having broken with the Ottomans, briefly rules Wallachia, Transylvania and Moldavia in a personal union.
Nicholas Mavrocordatos brings Phanariote rule to Wallachia; the Ottomans appoint its princes from the Greeks of Constantinople.
Tudor Vladimirescu's Pandur uprising enters Bucharest on 21 March; the turmoil ends Phanariote rule and restores local princes.
The Islaz Proclamation of 9 June and a Provisional Government depose Gheorghe Bibescu; Ottoman troops crush the revolution on 13 September.
Alexander John Cuza, already prince of Moldavia, is voted prince of Wallachia on 5 February, uniting the two principalities.

f.capital: Câmpulung, then Curtea de Argeș, Târgoviște and, after the late 17th century, Bucharest
f.founder: Basarab I, first ruler of the House of Basarab (tradition names the legendary Radu Negru)
f.predecessor: Vlach voivodates south of the Carpathians (Litovoi's Țara Litua, Bărbat) under Cuman, Bulgarian and Hungarian overlordship
f.successor: United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia (Romania from 1862, the Kingdom of Romania in 1881)
